author: Roger Lowenstein
biz: Run a correlation audit on your lead sources and lender panel

Long Term Capital held hundreds of positions that were really one bet. Ruby Holdings may be doing the same thing. This week, list every funded case from the last quarter by lead source and by lender, and ask what single event would hit several at once, such as a policy change across paid search, or two lenders tightening the same affordability criterion. Measure the share of funded volume coming from the largest single source and the largest single lender, and set a level above which you deliberately build an alternative before you need it.
Measure the outcome, not the model of it

The fund's risk reports said it was safe right up to the point it was not, because they described assumptions rather than reality. Apply that to Consumer Duty. This week, take a sample of recent cases flagged as showing vulnerability across both HomeownersLoan and Debt Support Direct, and check what actually happened to those customers rather than what the process assumes happened, including whether the product fit their circumstances and whether they understood the cost. Measure the gap between flagged and unflagged outcomes, and report that figure monthly.

b: John Meriwether was born in Chicago on the tenth of August 1947 and grew up on the South Side, in a settled Irish Catholic world of parish schools, small gardens and long winters. There was no family money for university. What there was, within reach of a bicycle, was a golf course, and from his early teens Meriwether carried other men's bags across it for a fee.

Caddying paid for his education. He won one of the scholarships American golf clubs endowed for exactly this purpose, and it took him to Northwestern University. He studied business, and by Roger Lowenstein's account spent a year teaching mathematics in a Chicago high school before taking a master's degree in business at the University of Chicago. A caddie is paid to be right about small quantities, repeatedly, without drawing attention to himself. Meriwether never really stopped.

In 1974 he joined Salomon Brothers in New York and was put on the repurchase desk, the plumbing of the bond market, where firms lend each other securities overnight against cash. It was the least glamorous room in the building. It was also where you learn what borrowing costs, and who will lend to you when the weather turns. Nobody could have guessed how much that second question would matter.

b: By the late 1970s Meriwether was running his own small group inside Salomon, trading what the firm called arbitrage. The word sounds exotic. The trade was dull. The American Treasury issues a thirty year bond, and six months later another. The older one is identical in almost every way but slightly harder to sell, so it trades a few hundredths of a per cent cheaper. Buy the cheap one, sell the dear one, and wait for them to converge.

Each trade earned a sliver. To live on slivers you had to trade in enormous size, which meant borrowing, and you had to be confident about when convergence would come. That is a mathematical question, so Meriwether went and bought mathematicians.

He recruited Eric Rosenfeld from Harvard Business School, then Victor Haghani, Larry Hilibrand, Gregory Hawkins and William Krasker. They were not traders in the old mould. They were quiet, argumentative and young, and trusted a regression more than a hunch. The floor called them the room of professors, resented them, and could not argue with the profits.

The resentment came to a head in 1990, when Hilibrand's share of the group's earnings reportedly reached around twenty three million dollars for the year. In a firm where senior partners earned a fraction of that, the number was an insult dressed as a pay slip.

Meriwether himself was becoming a legend, most famously through a story Michael Lewis told in Liar's Poker, in which the chairman John Gutfreund challenged him to one hand of the traders' bluffing game for a million dollars and Meriwether raised it to ten. He has always denied it happened. It is still repeated, which tells you how reputations get built out of stories nobody can verify.

b: Robert Merton was born in New York on the thirty first of July 1944 and raised in Hastings on Hudson, a village above the river. His father was a professor of sociology at Columbia who spent his life studying how societies produce consequences nobody intended. The son would spend his life on the same problem with different equipment.

The boy's first passion was baseball. At about eleven it became cars. At fifteen he bought his first car and rebuilt it, then built hot rods and raced them at drag strips, assuming he would be an automobile engineer. He spent two university summers at Ford in Dearborn.

A second obsession ran alongside. At ten or eleven he drew up a list of stocks he liked and bought his first share, in General Motors. In late 1963, still an undergraduate, he made his first risk arbitrage trade, buying one company and selling another short ahead of a merger. At Caltech he traded from a local brokerage at the opening bell.

He took a degree in engineering mathematics at Columbia in 1966 and a master's at Caltech in 1967, then decided economics was where his mathematics might actually matter. Of the departments he applied to, only one accepted him. He arrived at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the autumn of 1967, became Paul Samuelson's research assistant, and found the subject he had been circling all his life.

Merton's great contribution was this. If you can trade continuously, and prices move smoothly, you can build a portfolio of the underlying share and cash that behaves exactly like an option, adjusting it moment by moment. If you can manufacture the thing, you know what the thing is worth. Risk, in that framework, is not a mystery. It is a product with a cost of goods.

b: Myron Scholes was born on the first of July 1941 in Timmins, a gold mining town in northern Ontario where his father had gone to practise dentistry during the Depression. His mother and her uncle ran a chain of small department stores, and when the uncle died there was a quarrel over who owned what. Scholes called it his first encounter with contracts and incentives.

When he was ten the family moved some five hundred miles south to Hamilton. Soon after they arrived his mother developed cancer, and she died a few days after his sixteenth birthday. Then came a second blow. Scar tissue formed on both his corneas and his eyesight failed badly enough that sustained reading became impossible. A cornea transplant at twenty six restored it.

That decade of near blindness made him. Unable to read for long, he learned to hold problems in his head and strip them to their structure, and became by necessity an unusually good listener. Both habits show in his later work, which is famously spare.

He studied economics at McMaster University, graduated in 1962 and went to the University of Chicago, where one summer he took a programming job having never programmed in his life. Merton Miller suggested he join the doctoral programme. He worked alongside Eugene Fama, Michael Jensen and Richard Roll.

In 1968 he went to teach finance at the Sloan School in Cambridge, where he fell in with Fischer Black and with Merton. In 1973 Black and Scholes published the formula that bears their names, and Merton the paper that generalised it. It is one of the most consequential equations ever written, and it rests on an assumption that would one day matter more than anything else in it. The assumption is that you can always trade.

b: In 1991 Salomon Brothers was caught cheating in the auctions for United States government debt. The Treasury limited how much of an issue any one bidder could take, and Paul Mozer, who ran Salomon's government desk and reported to Meriwether, got round the limit by submitting bids in customers' names without their knowledge.

Mozer told Meriwether about a false bid in the spring of 1991. Meriwether took it immediately to the chairman, the president and the chief lawyer. There it stopped. Salomon's leadership did not tell the regulators for months, and when the story broke in August 1991 the delay was the scandal.

The firm nearly died. Warren Buffett, its largest shareholder, stepped in as interim chairman to stop the government withdrawing Salomon's licence to deal. Gutfreund resigned. So, in August 1991, did Meriwether, who had done the one thing the rules asked of him and reported upwards, and was still the supervisor of the man who cheated.

He later settled with the Securities and Exchange Commission over a failure to supervise, paying a civil penalty of fifty thousand dollars and accepting a suspension, without admitting or denying the finding. A small sum and a large wound.

Here is the first lesson of the book, and it arrives long before any mathematics. The thing that ended Meriwether's career at Salomon was not in any model. It was a man on his desk filling in a form dishonestly, and an organisation that then sat on the news. No equation prices that.

b: Meriwether spent two years assembling the best start up the hedge fund industry had seen. Most of the money was raised in late 1993, and Long Term Capital Management began trading on the twenty fourth of February 1994 from Greenwich, Connecticut, with a little over one billion dollars. Almost the entire old Salomon group came with him.

The names on the letterhead were extraordinary. Merton and Scholes were partners, as was David Mullins, until recently vice chairman of the Federal Reserve. Investors were asked for a minimum of ten million dollars, told they could not withdraw for three years, and charged two per cent a year plus twenty five per cent of profits, well above the going rate. They queued anyway.

The trades were the Salomon trades, industrialised. Italian government debt against swaps. Danish mortgage bonds. Later, selling insurance against large moves in share indices, in such volume that dealers began calling the fund the central bank of volatility.

Each position was a sliver. The engine that turned slivers into a fortune was borrowed money. If a trade earns one tenth of one per cent and you do it with twenty five pounds borrowed for every pound of your own, it earns you two and a half per cent. Leverage does not create the edge. It magnifies whatever is there, in both directions.

For three years the machine simply worked. After fees, investors made about twenty per cent in the first partial year, forty three per cent in 1995 and forty one per cent in 1996. The partners put almost all their own wealth into the fund, which everyone agreed was reassuring.

b: On the fourteenth of October 1997 the Royal Swedish Academy announced that Robert Merton and Myron Scholes had won that year's economics prize, for a new method to determine the value of derivatives. Fischer Black had died in 1995 and could not share it. Two partners of a private fund in Connecticut were now Nobel laureates.

The fund's own year was its weakest yet, about seventeen per cent after fees, which almost any manager alive would have taken gladly and which inside Long Term Capital felt like failure. The reason was ominous. Everyone was copying them.

This is the part that gets least attention and deserves most. A convergence trade works because few people are doing it. Once the big banks had built imitation arbitrage desks, often staffed by people the fund had trained, the gaps closed before Long Term Capital could reach them, and what remained was held by many firms at once. The trades looked diversified. They were the same bet, written in several languages.

At the end of 1997 the partners returned about two point seven billion dollars to outside investors, judging there were not enough good trades for the money. Their own capital stayed. Returning the cash reduced the equity without reducing the positions, so the leverage went up.

By the start of 1998 the fund had roughly four point seven billion dollars of capital supporting around one hundred and twenty nine billion of assets, and derivative contracts with a face value of about one and a quarter trillion. The risk models said this was comfortable, because the positions offset one another. They were describing a world in which markets stay open and sellers find buyers.
ch.cap: A Nobel arrives as the edge quietly erodes
ch.h: The Year They Won the Prize

b: The trouble began quietly. In May 1998 the fund lost about six per cent and in June about ten, its worst month to that point. Mortgage positions were going against it and nobody could see why.

On the seventeenth of August 1998 Russia defaulted on its domestic debt and let the rouble fall. The sum was small in global terms. The signal was not. Investors everywhere decided at the same moment that they wanted to hold the safest, most easily sold assets on earth, and nothing else.

This is called a flight to quality, and it is the opposite of convergence. Long Term Capital's trades were variations on one theme, that the cheap, awkward, illiquid thing would eventually be priced like the dear, liquid, famous one. In a panic that gap does not close. It yawns. Every position in the book moved the wrong way together.

On the twenty first of August the fund lost about half a billion dollars in a single day, taking its capital to around three point one billion. By the end of the month it was down about forty four per cent, some one point eight billion dollars, and it disclosed this to investors on the second of September.

Then the second trap closed. Losses triggered demands for more collateral from the banks that had lent the fund its securities. To raise cash it had to sell, but it held the unpopular side of every trade, and the only buyers were rival desks holding the same positions and facing the same calls. Selling pushed prices further against it. The mathematics of the trades had been fine. The mathematics of the exit had never been modelled.

b: By mid September the fund's capital was falling by hundreds of millions a week and Wall Street knew it. Every large bank was a counterparty, and several had copied the positions, so a forced liquidation would mark down their own books too. The fund was not too big to fail. It was too entangled to unwind.

A rescue was attempted from outside. Working through Goldman Sachs, Warren Buffett assembled a bid with Goldman and the insurer American International Group to buy the portfolio and inject fresh capital. Accounts of the terms differ, but on the twenty third of September Meriwether did not accept, saying he could not get the approvals in the time allowed. Buffett had given him about an hour.

That evening the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, under its president William McDonough, summoned the heads of the major banks. They met in lower Manhattan with a fund they had all financed on the brink of liquidating more than a trillion dollars of contracts into a frightened market.

The result was an agreement by fourteen institutions to put in about three point six billion dollars for ninety per cent of the fund, which would then be wound down under their supervision. Eleven firms put in three hundred million each, with smaller sums from three others. Bear Stearns, which cleared the fund's trades and had seen its books, refused outright.

It is important to be accurate about what this was. No public money was spent or formally at risk. The central bank supplied the room, the phone calls and the pressure. The banks supplied the cash, and were repaid when the portfolio was liquidated in early 2000. The partners, who had kept most of their fortunes in the fund, lost nearly everything.

b: The easy verdict, delivered everywhere in 1998, was that arrogant academics had believed their equations and the real world had corrected them. It is satisfying and mostly wrong, and the careful work done since says so.

The formula was not the problem. Black, Scholes and Merton stated their assumptions openly, and the central one was that you can trade continuously in a market that is there. What failed was everything the assumption excluded. Positions so large that selling them moved the price. Risk measures calibrated on a few calm years, which could not contain a month like August. Trades that looked independent in the statistics and were the same bet on tranquillity.

Scholes himself argued afterwards that the killer was liquidity risk rather than any error in pricing derivatives, and academic post mortems, notably Philippe Jorion's study of the episode, concluded much the same, pointing at position size, leverage and value at risk calculations built on short, quiet samples.

There is a deeper point underneath. Long Term Capital was selling insurance against disorder. In ordinary weather that business prints money and looks like genius, because the premiums arrive daily and the claims arrive never. The temptation, when a strategy wins ninety nine days in a hundred, is to decide you have found something safe and borrow more against it. What you have found is a bet whose rare loss erases every gain.

Meriwether raised money again in 1999 for a new fund, JWM Partners, which ran well for years and then lost about forty four per cent between September 2007 and February 2009, almost exactly the August 1998 figure, and closed in July 2009. He had rebuilt the machine with less leverage, and the same weather found it again.

The line usually quoted here is that markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent. It is attributed to John Maynard Keynes on no good evidence. The sentiment, at least, survived the test.
ch.cap: The real flaw was liquidity, not the formula
ch.h: What the Professors Actually Got Wrong

connects: Taleb's whole argument about rare, enormous events is written in the shadow of this collapse, where a month the models called impossible arrived anyway.
Fortune's Formula is about how much to bet when you have a real edge, and Long Term Capital is the clearest demonstration of what happens when you bet more than the edge can carry.
Against the Gods traces humanity's long effort to measure risk, and this story is the moment that effort met the one thing measurement cannot capture, the disappearance of the market itself.
note: The spine of this account is Roger Lowenstein's When Genius Failed, published in 2000 and based on his reporting rather than on insider access, so details of private meetings are reconstructions. Dates and figures here have been checked against the 1997 Nobel press release, the autobiographical essays Merton and Scholes wrote for the Nobel Foundation, and contemporary and reference accounts of the collapse; sources differ on the fund's exact opening capital, on the precise terms of the Buffett led bid of the twenty second and twenty third of September 1998, and on whether the consortium total was three point six or three point six two five billion dollars. The Liar's Poker hand between Gutfreund and Meriwether is a famous anecdote that Meriwether has denied, and the Keynes line about markets staying irrational is almost certainly not his.
recall: What was a convergence trade, in the form Long Term Capital used it?

It was a bet that two nearly identical securities priced slightly differently would come back into line. The fund would buy the cheaper, harder to sell one and sell the dearer, more liquid one, earning a tiny spread when they converged. Because each spread was tiny, the trade only paid if done in enormous, borrowed size.
What were the fund's capital and leverage at the start of 1998?

It had roughly four point seven billion dollars of its own capital supporting around one hundred and twenty nine billion dollars of assets, more than twenty five to one. On top of that sat derivative contracts with a face value of about one and a quarter trillion dollars.
What happened on the seventeenth of August 1998 and why did it matter so much?

Russia defaulted on its domestic debt and devalued the rouble. The direct exposure was modest, but it triggered a worldwide flight to quality in which investors dumped anything less than perfectly liquid, so every one of the fund's convergence trades widened at once instead of closing.
Who rescued Long Term Capital, and was public money used?

Fourteen banks, convened by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York under William McDonough on the twenty third of September 1998, put in about three point six billion dollars for ninety per cent of the fund. No public money was spent or formally at risk, and the banks were repaid when the portfolio was liquidated in early 2000.
According to later analysis, what actually failed, if not the Black Scholes formula?

Liquidity and position size. The pricing mathematics assumed you could always trade, while the fund held positions so large and so widely copied that selling them moved prices against itself. Risk measures calibrated on a few calm years could not represent a month like August 1998.
recap: Here is the story in miniature. John Meriwether, born in Chicago in 1947, caddied at a golf club to pay for university and arrived at Salomon Brothers in 1974. By the late 1970s he was running an arbitrage desk, and he did something nobody else had done. He hired academics. Eric Rosenfeld, Victor Haghani and Larry Hilibrand ran trades that bought the cheaper of two nearly identical bonds and sold the dearer, earning slivers in enormous, borrowed size. In 1991 a trader on his desk, Paul Mozer, was caught submitting false bids in Treasury auctions. Meriwether reported it upwards immediately, the firm sat on it, and when the story broke in August he resigned anyway. Two years later he built the fund that would carry everything he knew. Long Term Capital Management began trading on the twenty fourth of February 1994 from Greenwich, Connecticut, with just over a billion dollars, charging two per cent and twenty five per cent, demanding a ten million dollar minimum and a three year lock up. Robert Merton and Myron Scholes were partners, and in October 1997 they won the Nobel prize in economics for the option pricing work that underpinned the whole enterprise. For three years it returned around forty per cent a year after fees. Then the edge eroded, because every bank had copied the trades. At the end of 1997 the fund gave back two point seven billion dollars to investors without reducing its positions, so by early 1998 four point seven billion dollars of capital supported about one hundred and twenty nine billion of assets. On the seventeenth of August 1998 Russia defaulted. Investors fled to the safest assets on earth and every convergence trade widened at once. The fund lost about half a billion dollars on the twenty first of August and forty four per cent over the month, and selling to meet collateral calls pushed prices further against it. On the twenty third of September fourteen banks, convened by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, put in about three point six billion dollars for ninety per cent of the fund. No public money was used. The partners lost almost everything they had. The big ideas. Leverage magnifies a verdict rather than creating an edge. Positions that look diverse can be a single bet on calm. The exit is part of the trade, and in a panic there is no buyer. Models describe only the weather they were trained on. And a strategy that wins almost every day is usually selling insurance against the day it does not. The line to remember is this. They were not wrong about the prices. They were wrong about being able to sell.
stories: The pay slip that nearly broke Salomon

In 1990 Salomon Brothers paid Larry Hilibrand, a young quantitative trader on Meriwether's arbitrage desk, a share of profits reported at around twenty three million dollars for the year. Senior partners who had spent decades building the firm discovered that a man barely into his thirties, whom most of the floor could not pick out of a crowd, had out earned them many times over. The uproar was enormous and the resentment never really settled. The turn is that the number was arithmetically fair, a straight share of what his trades had made, and it still poisoned the place. Money paid by formula inside an organisation is never only money.
The hand of Liar's Poker that may never have happened

The most repeated story about John Meriwether is from Michael Lewis's book Liar's Poker. Salomon's chairman John Gutfreund supposedly walked onto the trading floor and challenged Meriwether to one hand of the traders' bluffing game for a million dollars, no tears. Meriwether, the story goes, looked up and said he would only play for ten million, and Gutfreund backed down. It is perfect, it is quoted in every profile, and Meriwether has always denied it happened. The point is not whether he said it. The point is that a reputation for nerve was worth more on that floor than any trade, so the market in stories was as active as the market in bonds.
The night Wall Street was summoned

On the evening of the twenty second of September 1998 the Federal Reserve Bank of New York telephoned the heads of the largest banks and told them to be in lower Manhattan within two hours. They came, sat around a table, and were asked to bail out a private fund in Connecticut run by sixteen people. The turn is why they agreed. Every one of them had lent to it, several had copied its trades, and a fire sale of one and a quarter trillion dollars of contracts would have marked down their own books too. Bear Stearns, which cleared the fund's trades and had seen the books most closely, refused outright. Within ten years Bear Stearns itself was gone.
take: Leverage does not create an edge, it enlarges a verdict
Work out what a bad month would do to you at your current level of borrowing before you work out what a good one would pay. If the bad month ends you, the good month is irrelevant.
Positions that look diverse can be one bet
Ask what single condition would have to be true for all your holdings, income streams or customers to suffer at once. Diversification measured in names is not diversification measured in causes.
The exit is part of the trade
Before committing, ask who the buyer will be on the day you most want to sell. If the answer is people in exactly your position, you do not have a position, you have a trap.
Models describe the weather they were trained on
A risk estimate built on three calm years cannot tell you about the fourth year. Treat any number derived from a short, quiet history as a lower bound on trouble, never a ceiling.
Winning almost every day is a warning as well as a reward
Strategies that earn small, steady sums are often selling insurance against something rare. Find out what the rare thing is, and price the day it happens.
Returning capital while keeping positions raises your risk
Any time you shrink the cushion without shrinking the exposure, you have quietly increased your leverage. Check the ratio, not just the balance.
Reputation and process risk sit outside every model
Meriwether's first career ended because a subordinate filled in a form dishonestly. Supervision, reporting lines and the speed of bad news travelling upwards are real risk controls, not paperwork.
Survival is the first objective, returns are the second
Size every commitment so that being wrong is survivable, because the long run only pays people who are still there for it.
title: The Trade That Could Not Lose
wiifm: You are about to watch the cleverest men in finance borrow their way to ruin in five weeks, and see exactly where the thinking went wrong. By the end you will know why a strategy that wins almost every day can still destroy you, why borrowed money turns a small mistake into a final one, and why the moment everybody wants out is the moment there is no out. If you run a business with thin margins and fixed costs, this is not a story about hedge funds. It is a story about survival.
words: Profiting from the same thing being priced differently in two places, in principle without taking a risk on the price itself.
Long Term Capital's whole book was arbitrage, buying the cheap version of a bond and selling the dear one, which stopped being riskless the moment it could not sell.
Using borrowed money so that a given amount of your own capital controls a much larger position.
At more than twenty five to one, a four per cent move against the fund's assets was enough to wipe out its entire capital.
How easily something can be sold for close to its quoted value without moving the price.
The fund owned the illiquid side of nearly every trade, so in the panic its assets were worth far less than the screens said.
The degree to which two things move together.
Positions that had looked unrelated for years became almost perfectly correlated in August 1998, because they were all really bets on calm markets.
Overreaching pride that invites the downfall it cannot imagine.
Two Nobel laureates, a former vice chairman of the Federal Reserve and the finest traders on Wall Street still managed to build a fund that could not survive one bad autumn.
